## 1a. A table that started a national crisis

In October 2024, the Uganda Bureau of Statistics (UBOS) published the
provisional results of the National Population and Housing Census.^[Daily
Monitor, "Ubos withdraws census report following public concerns".
<https://www.monitor.co.ug/uganda/news/national/ubos-withdraws-census-report-following-public-concerns-4787808>
(accessed 5 October 2026). The report went online on 3 October 2024.] One
table — the population by tribe — set off a storm.

![Provisional census figures, as published](images/census-2024-bad-table.jpeg)

Look at the table for a moment. Does anything strike you as odd?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What happened

Several tribes' 2014 baseline figures did not match the 2014 census. The
figures for four tribes had been transposed — each tribe given another
tribe's number — making their ten-year growth look impossible. UBOS
withdrew the report and reissued corrected figures.^[Eagle Online, "UBOS
retracts 2024 census report over ethnic group data errors", 8 October 2024.
<https://eagle.co.ug/2024/10/08/ubos-retracts-2024-census-report-over-ethnic-group-data-errors/>
(accessed 5 October 2026). The corrected figures are in the UBOS final
report: [National Population and Housing Census 2024, Final Report, Volume 1
(Main)](https://www.ubos.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/National-Population-and-Housing-Census-2024-Final-Report-Volume-1-Main.pdf).]

We will come back to this story, and this data, throughout the workshop.
:::

## 1b. One idea behind all of it

Every visualisation — every plot, every table, every dashboard — is a
**mapping from data values to visual properties**.

| Data value  | Visual property                  |
|-------------|----------------------------------|
| a number    | a position along an axis         |
| a category  | a colour, a shape                |
| a magnitude | a length, an area, a font weight |

That is the whole idea. The rest of the workshop is about learning to see
it, and to use it deliberately.

### Choosing a mapping

Some visual properties are easier to read accurately than others. In a
classic study of graphical perception,^[Cleveland, W. S. and McGill, R.
(1984). Graphical perception: Theory, experimentation, and application to
the development of graphical methods. *Journal of the American Statistical
Association*, 79(387), 531–554.
<https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478080>] people judged numbers
best from the properties at the top of this list:

1. position along a shared axis
2. length
3. angle or slope
4. area
5. colour shade

Use the properties near the top for the values readers must compare
precisely. Use colour for categories, or for a value that only needs a
rough reading.

## 1c. What maps to what?

For each visualisation below, ask: **which data column maps to which
visual property?** Discuss with a neighbour, then open the answer.

### A bar chart

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of the ten most populous African countries in 2007, with bars coloured by region. Nigeria is the longest bar at 135 million."
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *
from great_tables import GT

gapminder_2007 = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_africa_2007.csv")
gapminder = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_africa.csv")

top = gapminder_2007.nlargest(10, "pop").copy()
top["country"] = pd.Categorical(top.country, categories=top.sort_values("pop").country)
(
    ggplot(top, aes(x="country", y="pop", fill="region"))
    + geom_col()
    + coord_flip()
    + scale_y_continuous(labels=lambda s: [f"{x/1e6:.0f}M" for x in s])
    + labs(x="", y="Population, 2007", fill="Region",
           title="Africa's ten most populous countries")
    + theme(figure_size=(7, 4))
)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Data column | Visual property                  |
|-------------|----------------------------------|
| country     | vertical position (one bar each) |
| population  | bar length                       |
| region      | bar colour                       |

The bars are also *sorted* by population: order is a mapping too.
:::

### A heat map

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Heat map of life expectancy in eight East African countries from 1952 to 2007. Each tile is coloured from dark purple (low) to yellow (high). Rwanda's 1992 tile is the darkest."
east = gapminder[gapminder.region == "Eastern Africa"]
east = east[east.country.isin(
    ["Burundi", "Eritrea", "Ethiopia", "Kenya", "Rwanda", "Somalia", "Tanzania", "Uganda"]
)]
(
    ggplot(east, aes(x="factor(year)", y="country", fill="lifeExp"))
    + geom_tile(color="white")
    + labs(x="", y="", fill="Life\nexpectancy", title="Life expectancy in East Africa")
    + theme(figure_size=(8, 3.5))
)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Data column     | Visual property     |
|-----------------|---------------------|
| year            | horizontal position |
| country         | vertical position   |
| life expectancy | tile colour         |

Position places each tile; colour carries the value.
:::

### A table

```{python}
selected = gapminder_2007[gapminder_2007.country.isin(
    ["Egypt", "Ghana", "Kenya", "Morocco", "Nigeria", "Rwanda", "Senegal", "Uganda"]
)]
selected = selected.sort_values(["region", "lifeExp"], ascending=[True, False]).reset_index(drop=True)
(
    GT(selected[["country", "region", "lifeExp", "pop", "gdpPercap"]],
       rowname_col="country", groupname_col="region")
    .tab_header(title="Selected countries, 2007")
    .fmt_number(columns="lifeExp", decimals=1)
    .fmt_number(columns="pop", scale_by=1e-6, decimals=1, pattern="{x}M")
    .fmt_currency(columns="gdpPercap", decimals=0)
    .data_color(columns="lifeExp", palette="viridis")
    .cols_label(lifeExp="Life expectancy", pop="Population", gdpPercap="GDP per person")
)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Data column     | Visual property             |
|-----------------|-----------------------------|
| region          | row grouping                |
| country         | row label                   |
| life expectancy | cell colour *and* text      |
| population      | text, formatted in millions |
| GDP per person  | text, formatted as currency |

A table maps data too: to text, formatting, grouping and order. The
coloured column is the same mapping as the heat map above: value →
colour, on the same colour scale.
:::

## 1d. Same mapping, new coordinates

A bar chart and a pie chart look like different kinds of chart. Here is one
stacked bar of the five most populous African countries:

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "One tall stacked bar of the five most populous African countries in 2007, split by country. Nigeria is the largest segment at the top; South Africa is the smallest at the bottom."
top5 = gapminder_2007.nlargest(5, "pop").copy()
top5["country"] = pd.Categorical(
    top5.country, categories=top5.sort_values("pop", ascending=False).country
)
stacked = (
    ggplot(top5, aes(x=1, y="pop", fill="country"))
    + geom_col(width=1)
    + scale_x_continuous(expand=(0, 0))
    + scale_y_continuous(
        expand=(0, 0), labels=lambda s: [f"{x/1e6:.0f}M" for x in s]
    )
    + labs(x="", y="Population, 2007", fill="Country")
    + theme(
        figure_size=(5, 4),
        axis_text_x=element_blank(),
        axis_ticks_major_x=element_blank(),
    )
)
stacked
```

Now draw the same bar in radial coordinates:

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Pie chart of the five most populous African countries in 2007. Nigeria has the largest slice, about a third. Egypt, Ethiopia and DR Congo have slices of similar size."
stacked + coord_radial(theta="y") + theme_void()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What changed?

Nothing in the mapping. In both charts:

| Data column | Visual property |
|-------------|-----------------|
| country     | colour          |
| population  | size of segment |

Radial coordinates bend the bar into a circle, so each segment's *length*
becomes an *angle*.

Compare Egypt, Ethiopia and DR Congo in each chart. Length is easier to
judge than angle (see 1b), so the differences are clearer in the bar.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## The question to keep asking

A plot and a table are not different kinds of thing. Both answer the same
question: **what maps to what?** We'll ask it of every visualisation in
this workshop, starting with plots in Part 2.
:::
